body:
Hi

Thanks for reporting. I think this may be a global problem of the functions actually.
Let's wait for mike here.

Did you test also on 1.4?
Yes, same behavior for 1.4.

it can't be for functions globally because we have a crapload of tests.      Side note it looks like I forgot to add a `__ne__` method to CacheKey() which makes quick testing of this quite annoying, so we should add that also here, but a working test is:

```py
from sqlalchemy import func


x = func.foo_bar(1, 2, 3)
y = func.foo_bar(4, 5, 6)
z = func.foo_bar_bat(1, 2, 3)


assert x._generate_cache_key().key == y._generate_cache_key().key

assert x._generate_cache_key().key != z._generate_cache_key().key

assert not (x._generate_cache_key().key == z._generate_cache_key().key)


```
regexp_match is an operator, not a function, so this is not related to functions anyway

so the BinaryElement caches the "flags" as "modifiers" and "modifiers" is not expected to be SQL expressions, it's expected to be constants that are directly cacheable.    at the moment I'm leaning towards keeping that going and not using bound parameters for these flags, but I might reverse course on that.

the other example of "modifiers" are the "escapes" used by LIKE and similar opts.  these are present in the modifiers dictionary directly as strings.      I think we should go with that approach here which requires changes to the compiler, etc.

we might want to add a coercion here that ensures no quote characters are present
OK we dont need coercsion, we render them as safestirngs in the compiler, great

ok change of plans again, the "replacement" expression is also placed in the "modifiers".   OK.   I...might want to change that.   I think we need dedicated construct, "modifiers" is not supposed to be used this way

> regexp_match is an operator, not a function, so this is not related to functions anyway

sorry, yes. I meant that's probably something shared by other similar operators

> ok change of plans again, the "replacement" expression is also placed in the "modifiers". OK. I...might want to change that. I think we need dedicated construct, "modifiers" is not supposed to be used this way

dedicated construct seems to be the best option here

OK, I have 99% of this working without any new construct.

however.   we have tests with PostgresqL sending a column into "flags".  What's that about?  can we just not support that ?  who would ever do that?

I don't remember if it was requested or not. pg does support anything everywhere, it just need to have the correct type

I think support for it can be removed and if there are requests it can be re-visited
(should error in that case though)

**Mike Bayer** has proposed a fix for this issue in the **main** branch:

**remove use of SQL expressions in "modifiers" for regexp** https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/4758
what are the chances we think a third party dialect in 1.4 is using these regexp constructs?  because i have proposed changing their structure to work the way "between" works

> what are the chances we think a third party dialect in 1.4 is using these regexp constructs? because i have proposed changing their structure to work the way "between" works

haven't checked them but according to github here are 350 matches of visit_regexp_match_op_binary
https://github.com/search?q=visit_regexp_match_op_binary++path%3A*.py+language%3APython&type=Code&ref=advsearch&l=Python&l=
yes that search is useless because thousands of projects vendor SQLAlchemy in their github repos

I'd like to go forward and change this to be how I think it should be and if we get regressions from 3rd parties we can help them at that point.   This is at least a way that we get alerted that 3rd parties are even implementing their own regex operators (which I'd wager nobody is right now)
but i need info on why PG is putting a column expression into "modifiers" and if that is a real use case (looks like not)
Can you point to the change that added this feature?
b1b97ed1fcac777c4f42f

It's likely that it's just a test thing I added.
I can't think of a real use case here
OK.   just going to go w it....

also this is not just the flags but the replacement expression also

i know that if I just made "modifiers" cached on SQL expressions that would also fix this, but that was not the intended use of this dictionary....

More of an use case may be made for replacement compared to flags, but I'm not sure how likely this would be still.

Are there no other cases where there are similar modifiers for operators that may benefit from that feature?
